title: Packetization vs Application-level Chunking: Exploratory Notes
content:
Purpose:
This is an exploratory notes doc to capture experiments and hypotheses about where streaming latency and CPU overhead come from when we: 1) let the OS/net stack do packetization (small writes, TCP/Nagle behavior), vs 2) application-level chunking (coalesced writes of larger buffers), and 3) how intermediate proxies (Envoy/nginx) and gRPC vs HTTP/1.1/2 affect tail latency and backpressure.

Context / motivation:
- Multiple customer reports of spiky p95s when using streaming endpoints behind our edge proxies.
- Recent infra changes (kernel bump, default TCP settings) might have changed interaction with Nagle/TCP_NODELAY.
- We suspect a mixture of small-write overhead, TLS record flush frequency, and proxy buffering heuristics are amplifying latency on small token streams.

Hypotheses to test (rough prioritization):
1) Small application writes (1–4KB) that rely on the kernel to packetize lead to higher CPU per-token and higher p95 due to syscalls and TLS record count.
2) Coalescing at the app level into 16–64KB chunks reduces syscall/TLS overhead and improves throughput but risks higher per-chunk serialization latency (when tokens are generated slowly).
3) Proxies (Envoy/nginx) with buffer thresholds cause head-of-line delays: they may buffer until X bytes or timeout before flushing, converting many small chunks into infrequent larger writes (good for bandwidth, bad for latency).
4) gRPC (HTTP/2) stream multiplexing plus frame coalescing interacts with flow control windows causing different tail behavior vs HTTP/1.1 chunked responses.

Environment & test harness:
- Serving binary: serving-runtime:v3.7.2-debug (build flags: debug-profiling on)
- Models: small decoder-only test-model (synth latency ~25ms per chunk) to isolate network overhead from model compute.
- Clients: 10k RPS warmup, then synthetic streaming sessions (n=1k concurrent streams) using a token emitter script.
- Network: k8s clusters across two zones; tests done both without proxy (direct LB -> instance) and with Envoy sidecars + edge nginx.
- TLS: AWS/Cloud certs, TLS1.3 default.
- Kernel tweaks tested: tcp_nodelay on/off, net.ipv4.tcp_low_latency toggles, mss adjustments.

Test matrix (examples):
- App write sizes: 512B, 2KB, 8KB, 32KB.
- Write strategy: immediate write (each token), coalesced-buffer (flush every X ms or X bytes), adaptive (flush when KV-cache hit).
- Proxy: none, Envoy sidecar default, Envoy tuned (flush-on-every-data frame), Nginx (proxy_buffering on/off).
- Protocol: HTTP/1.1 chunked, HTTP/2 (gRPC) streaming (headers+DATA frames).
- Congestion: normal (no packet loss) vs induced 1% packet loss + 10ms jitter.

Key metrics captured:
- p50/p95/p99 end-to-end latency (client observed).
- Server-side CPU % spent in syscall/tls crypto vs model compute (from perf/ebpf samples).
- Number of TLS records per response and average TLS record size.
- Syscall counts (write/sendmsg) per stream.
- Envoy/nginx flush counts and buffer hold durations.
- Bandwidth and bytes-on-wire overhead.

Preliminary results (small synthetic runs):
- Direct (no proxy), HTTP/1.1, immediate writes at ~1k streams:
  - 512B writes: p50=9ms, p95=48ms, p99=210ms; avg TLS records per stream=~45; syscalls per stream =~60.
  - 8KB writes (coalesced): p50=8ms, p95=22ms, p99=60ms; tls records per stream=~6; syscalls ~=8.
- With Envoy (default):
  - 512B writes: p50=12ms, p95=120ms, p99=430ms; observed Envoy buffer hold time spikes (flush intervals ~100ms)
  - 8KB writes: p95 comparable to direct case, p99 improved vs small writes.
- gRPC/HTTP2 differences (direct):
  - gRPC frames (small writes mapped to DATA frames) showed slightly better p50 but worse p95 when many streams multiplexed -> evidence of stream-level flow control stalls.

Observations / notes:
- TLS record count correlates strongly with CPU overhead. More small writes -> many small TLS records -> more cipher ops and more per-record overhead.
- Envoy's default path introduces a buffering heuristic that tries to amortize syscalls; when workloads are bursty and small, it increases tail latencies because it waits for a threshold or a timer before flushing.
- For gRPC, we saw both pros and cons: multiplexing reduces connection count cost but exposes head-of-line stalls at flow-control granularity; tuning INITIAL_WINDOW/flow-control helped but we need systematic safety checks for memory blowouts.
- Nagle/TCP_NODELAY: enabling TCP_NODELAY at the server drastically reduced p95 for direct connections with small writes, but proxies sometimes ignored the flag or changed behavior (Envoy may set its own socket options on upstream).

Quick wins to try (actionable):
- Add an adaptive flushing layer in runtime: coalesce up to 8–16KB or flush earlier if token inter-arrival > X ms. This balances latency for slow tokens and syscall/TLS cost for fast tokens. (Owner: Amrita)
- Instrument TLS record sizes and expose a metric: tls.records_per_stream (Owner: Diego)
- For Envoy: test explicit configuration to flush on write (disable proxy buffering heuristics) for streaming routes; measure memory/backpressure impact. (Owner: Lucas)
- Add eBPF-based syscall counters to production canaries to validate real traffic behavior before broad rollout. (Owner: SRE pairing)

Open questions / risks:
- Does coalescing increase perceived latency for interactive users when tokens are generated slowly? We need UX benchmarks with realistic token timing distributions.
- Memory pressure under Envoy flush-on-every-write for high concurrency. Need to model worst-case concurrent open streams * buffered bytes.
- TLS overhead tradeoffs vs enabling TLS record size limits or using 0-RTT style session resumption optimizations.
- Interaction with client libraries: some client gRPC implementations coalesce on their side; fighting client-side coalescing could be counterproductive.

Immediate next experiments (this sprint):
1) Implement adaptive-flush prototype in runtime (8KB max, 10ms max delay) and run A/B with traffic replay for three customer workloads.
2) Envoy tuning matrix: disable buffering, set flush timer to 1ms, test memory; enable early flush and measure p99 and mem usage.
3) Kernel flags matrix: tcp_nodelay on/off; test TLS write coalescing behavior.

Notes to reviewers:
- This doc is exploratory and contains rough numbers from quick experiments. Numbers will change with larger sample size. Please paste links to related tickets or customer traces into linked_artifacts.
- If anyone has a curated corpus of realistic token emission timings (customer X vs chatty demo app), drop it in CONFLUENCE STREAM-interop page so we can replay realistic sessions.

Appendix (short):
- Tools used: wrk-like token emitter, tcpdump+Wireshark for TLS record counts (decrypt with test certs), perf + bpftrace scripts for syscall attribution.
- Relevant tickets: INF-4821 (edge p95), INF-4873 (envoy flush bug), PERF-221 (syscall profiling harness).
